title: The vibe-coded UI isn’t the issue with “AI quant backtesters".... the backend is, and only a few sites have actually built one that goes beyond the backtest.
author: person-person12
selftext:
The “AI quant” space is getting buried in **software-shaped slop.** The same looking sites with the same Lovable watermark, same landing page, and same promise that you can “**Become a quant overnight and backtest anything with AI.**” Then you look do some digging and realize how many of them are **far less substantial than the UI makes them look** as AI has made it incredibly easy to produce a polished trading interface.  **Where that progress hasn’t carried over nearly as much is the backend** which that is where the difference becomes obvious: weaker infrastructure, fewer real systems, and often no comprehensive path from backtest to execution.

And before someone says “AI-generated website,” **that is not my criticism.** I own [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/) and we use AI in our frontend development.

**Generating frontend code is not the hard part anymore.** Last yr Anthropic found that AI is hitting frontend work far faster than backend engineering, stating that *“simple applications and user interfaces may face disruption from AI systems sooner than those focused purely on backend work”* (**Anthropic, 2025**).

What’s even more important is that **AI-written code is becoming standard practice in professional software development.** Sundar Pichai reported this year that *“75% of all new code at Google is now AI-generated and* ***approved*** *by engineers”* (**Swartz, 2026**) and Klarna has used generative AI to produce more than 1,000 campaign images while significantly cutting production costs (**Klarna, 2024**). Pull up the home page for Robinhood, Coinbase or Stripe today and plenty of people would tell you those look AI-generated despite them being huge industry names with more than enough money to spend on devs. Everything looks the same now, professional or not, which is exactly why **the way a site looks tells you nothing.**

It's because of this that I think it's silly to criticize someone for not manually writing out lines of JavaScript UI for every page in their platform, **its not the 90s anymore. The question is whether there is real engineering underneath it,** which is why the word **“approved”** is bold in that Google quote. Whether somebody used AI to write their React components tells you almost nothing about whether the product is serious. The hard part is the **architecture, data, testing, execution and production infra/systems** underneath it.

The UI being the easy part now is exactly why there are suddenly so many “**AI quant backtesters**” with Lovable watermarks popping up every day which **is not what bothers me.** The issue is what happens after you press Run. **Market data, security, deterministic backtesting, job infrastructure, strategy versioning, broker connections, risk controls, live position state, execution and failure handling are the actual product.** Architecture and implementation for a system like this is extensive and took my team thousands of both dollars and hours to build.

*(For reference, the table below shows what we actually compute in a backtest* ***and what the live automation layer does after it.****)*

The entire reason you backtest something in code is to **remove discretion.** The strategy enters when the rule says enter and doesn't hesitate, move a stop early, skip Monday bc Friday sucked or enter two candles late. But... if the backtest ends and there is no way to paper trade or execute that exact logic... **what was the point?** You removed yourself from the strategy to prove whether it worked, then put yourself right back in charge of executing it.

QuantPad is a great counterexample here because it has the same kind of AI-era SaaS look that suddenly turns everyone into a professional UI critic, **but underneath it is genuinely serious research software**, which is exactly why I think judging these products by the frontend is useless. As the founder of a somewhat comparable platform I have no problem giving them credit for that, but  I would like to acknowledge a separate limitation.   With it being an IDE/research environment, you can validate a strategy extremely well but with no native path to execute that same strategy directly into paper or live markets.

So that is really how I see the market right now:   
  
1) **the low-effort end gives you generated code and a backtest**  
**2) the serious research end gives you much better answers but still usually stops before execution.**   
  
Because of this outlook, **Agenticks is designed specifically to take the same strategy through the full process; from research, rules, backtesting and validation to walk-forward analysis and live automation.**  
  
That is where the market splits in a way I think is **useful**. A lot of the low-effort “AI backtesters” are basically **strategy-to-script wrappers**: you describe an idea, an LLM writes Pine v6 *(or similar)* code, somebody else’s engine runs the test, and you leave with a script or report but no execution layer behind it. QuantPad sits at the opposite end: **genuinely sophisticated research** infrastructure, but **still primarily research.**

**Agenticks is trying to connect those two halves.** The strategy is turned into explicit rules and Python, shown back to you before it runs, backtested and stress-tested, and then that **same strategy** can continue into paper or live execution through your connected brokerage under limits you control.

*(The attached video shows that flow pretty quickly.)*

Just to summarize my opinion: **looking AI-generated tells you almost nothing about whether a piece of software is actually good anymore.** Frontend has become dramatically easier to produce; the real distinction is what has actually been engineered underneath it and how far the product carries the user once they press Run.

And on the trading side specifically, I do not think a backtest should be the product. It should be a step:

**idea → rules → code → backtest → stress test → paper → live**

Some products stop at generating the script. Some build genuinely serious research infrastructure but stop before execution. Either way, if the software stops halfway through that chain, **the user is still responsible for building or manually replacing the part that comes next.**

For people who actually build or use these tools: **what separates a real platform from a wrapper to you, and what do you actually do with the strategy after the backtest?**

comments.author: SecretCGG
comments.body: The real differentiator is what happens after you hit **Run**. A polished UI can be generated quickly now, but reliable data, backtesting, risk controls, execution, and production infrastructure are what actually make a trading platform serious. The idea → backtest → paper → live pipeline is a much better benchmark than judging a product by how its frontend looks.
